newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Data may understate Australia Q4 GDP-analysts.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Data may understate Australia Q4 GDP-analysts.

text.p: The Australian economy may prove to have been much stronger than Thursday's weak December quarter GDP data suggested, some economists said.
Their arguments suggest the underlying driving force behind GDP -- private consumption and investment -- was stronger than the figures showed.
Analysts said Q4 private final demand, which was stronger than GDP itself, would have been stronger still had there not been big second-hand asset transactions in the previous quarter.
The statistics bureau's problems with retail seasonality may have also led to private demand being understated.
"I don't think things were that bad," said Citibank economist Annette Beacher, noting the 0.5 percent December quarter rise in GDP.
Macquarie Bank chief economist Bill Shields said the quarter's big fall in labour productivity -- to just 2.4 percent from a downwardly revised 3.3 percent -- was improbable.
So either estimates of hours worked should be revised down or, more likely, production would go up, he said.
Lending weight to the possibility of a major revision of Q4 GDP, is the fact that the discrepancy between income and expenditure measures of GDP blew out in the quarter to A$1.7 billion.

Bankers Trust chief economist Chris Caton pointed out, however, that the very large statistical discrepancy showed only that something might be wrong in the data, not the direction that any revision would take.
The 0.5 percent GDP growth was an average of the Australian Bureau of Statistics's three primary measures of GDP -- income, expenditure and production (GDP-I, -E and -P).
But within GDP-I private final demand rose 0.7 percent in the December quarter from the previous quarter.
A bureau official pointed to that growth rate having been suppressed by an unusually strong September quarter.
In the September quarter, the private sector bought several large second-hand assets from state governments, massively boosting figures for non-dwelling construction.
Macquarie calculated that if the asset sales were discounted then private final demand would have risen 1.1 percent in the quarter, equivalent to an annualised rate near 4.5 percent.
But this analysis suggested strength in the December quarter only at the expense of the previous quarter.
Caton said that if the asset sales were ignored then the September quarter would have to be counted that much weaker.
Economists suspect the bureau is having trouble with changing seasonality in retail trade.
"Consumers have moved from pre-Christmas to post-Christmas purchases," said Shields.
If the bureau's seasonal adjustment process had not caught up with that change in behaviour, then it would see what was now normal spending as weak in December and strong in January.
This is the pattern that has appeared in recent retail data.

If the seasonal adjustment process is indeed depressing December retail trade too far, then December quarter consumption would also suffer, although Caton pointed out that this was a smaller issue for the quarterly GDP figures than for the monthly turnover data.
The bureau has looked at the problem in recent years but officials told Reuters on Thursday they were unable to say whether they still had problems with consumption seasonality.
But the officials rejected the argument that the rapid fall in labour productivity implied that December quarter GDP would be revised up.
Earlier studies had shown it was normal for production to rise before employment, meaning that productivity would usually spike up before falling as job numbers caught up with output.
